name: Mure
confidence_why: Mure is extinct and survives only in three unaccented eighteenth-century prayer texts printed by Teza (1868) and re-edited by Créqui-Montfort & Rivet (1913), so no source describes its stress from Mure data; Angenot (2013) states a weight-based stress rule for the whole Chapakura family and counts Muré in it, but gives no Mure evidence, and Glottolog classifies Mure as an isolate whose Chapakura look-alikes are loans.

Protochapakura'); Muré listed as language no. 20 of the family on p. 12; Mure section 3.12 pp. 61-62 (source: Créqui-Montfort & Rivet 1913; phoneme tables and length-marked examples, no stress marks); acoustic tables pp. 148-149 cover Miguelenho, More, Kuyubi, Oro Mon, Oro Win only. All pages re-extracted with from the PDF (159 pp.). In the low/high tone marks on σ render as ò/è, the stress mark as », vowel length as ˘, the breve on light CV as '(' and the non-syllabic mark on the second V of CVV as '9'. Créqui-Montfort & Rivet 1913 checked in the copy consulted (Mure grammatical observations pp. 137-138, Mure texts pp. 168-169); Glottolog family-membership comment checked in the copy consulted.
catalog_quote: Nas línguas Chapakura, a acentuação dos lexemas é dedutível do peso silábico - o único fator prosódico fonológico nessa família lingüística. Portanto, o acento não é fonológico por ser previsível. ... A atualização fonética da acentuação lexical obedece às seguintes regras: (a) uma sílaba leve é átona e possui um tom baixo. Em outras palavras, carrega um acento de intensidade (“stress”) fraco e um acento de altura (“pitch”) baixo; (b) uma sílaba pesada é tônica e possui um tom alto. Em outras palavras, carrega um acento de intensidade (“stress”) forte e um acento de altura (“pitch”) alto. / # (σ) σ # / → [ (σò) » σè] ... O fator demarcativo do lexema é, portanto, o peso silábico, uma vez que uma sílaba pesada caracteriza sempre o final de um lexema, ao passo que uma sílaba leve caracteriza sempre a primeira sílaba de um lexema dissílabo. ... Quanto à acentuação lexical, mostramos que ela é dedutível do peso silábico: a nível lexical, a sílaba leve é sempre não-acentuada e a sílaba pesada é sempre acentuada. Em função do comportamento homogêneo das diversas línguas Chapakura, consideramos que a situação atestada atualmente já imperava em Protochapakura.

new_statements.translation: In the Chapakura languages, the stress of lexemes is deducible from syllable weight - the only phonological prosodic factor in this language family. Therefore stress is not phonological, since it is predictable. [...] (a) a light syllable is unstressed and has a low tone; in other words, it carries weak intensity accent ('stress') and low pitch accent; (b) a heavy syllable is stressed and has a high tone; in other words, it carries strong intensity accent ('stress') and high pitch accent. /#(σ)σ#/ → [(σ̀) ˈσ́]

Surrounding section 2.1.1 (pp. 21-22) confirms the grounding: lexemes are # (σ) σ #, a disyllabic lexeme is always light+heavy, a monosyl…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no record and no prior stress statement for Mure. This work supplies one only by extension: the weight-based, non-contrastive stress rule is asserted for 'as línguas Chapakura' as a whole and the author explicitly counts Muré among the 13 documented Chapakura languages (p. 4); nothing in the Mure section itself, and nothing in the three 18th-century mission texts that are the entire Mure corpus, bears on stress. Note Glottolog classifies mure1235 as an isolate, not Chapacuran.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level claim: every Chapakura lexeme is either a single heavy syllable (CVC, CV:, CVV) or a light syllable (CV) followed by a heavy one; the heavy syllable is always lexeme-final (p. 22: 'uma sílaba pesada caracteriza sempre o final de um lexema') and is the one that carries stress and high pitch, so stress is predictable from weight and in practice lexeme-final; stress is non-contrastive and serves only to demarcate lexemes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; lexemes are at most disyllabic, so no secondary stress arises.
new_statements.exceptions: In casual/hypoarticulated registers stressed vowels shorten and monosyllabic lexemes fuse, so one phonological word can span up to three lexemes (pp. 22-23). Acoustic study (pp. 148-149) reports Oro Mon has moved high pitch onto the light first syllable ('metátese da altura') while intensity stays on the heavy syllable; that is Oro Mon, not Mure. The Mure-specific section 3.12 (pp. 61-62, based only on Créqui-Montfort & Rivet 1913) gives phonemes and examples with no stress marks at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Angenot 2013 treats Muré as a Chapakura language of the Bolivian Moxos missions (mission of San Miguel, mouth of the Rio Blanco; p. 8 list item 20), documented only by the Pater Noster, Ave Maria and Credo printed by Teza 1868 and re-edited by Créqui-Montfort & Rivet 1913. Glottolog lists mure1235 as an isolate. The stress statement is about the whole Chapakura family, not a Mure dialect.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources (only one work was listed and opened). The only tension is evidential: Angenot 2013 states a family-wide rule (stress predictable from syllable weight, on the heavy lexeme-final syllable, non-contrastive) and includes Muré in the family, but the Mure-specific section carries no stress marks and its sole source (Créqui-Montfort & Rivet 1913, re-editing Teza 1868's unaccented Pater/Ave/Credo) cannot show stress; the acoustic verification (pp. 148-149) covers only living languages (Moré, Kuyubi, Miguelenho-Wanham, Oro Win, Oro Mon). The prior check's conclusion that no source states anything about Mure stress from Mure data still stands; Angenot's statement applies to Mure by classification, and Glottolog does not accept that classification (isolate).
